scenes.tts: In an adult human at rest, blood leaves the heart in arteries, passes through arterioles and capillaries, and returns in veins. It moves fastest in the aorta, the widest artery. It moves slowest in the capillaries, the narrowest vessels in the body. That sounds backward, like a river slowing where it narrows. So why is blood slowest in the smallest vessels?
scenes.visual: A wide aorta bar with a fast arrow, then a branching bed of thin capillary bars with a slow arrow and a question mark.
scenes.narration: In an adult human at rest, blood leaves the heart in arteries, passes through arterioles and capillaries, and returns in veins. It moves fastest in the aorta, the widest artery. It moves slowest in the capillaries, the narrowest vessels in the body. That sounds backward, like a river slowing where it narrows. So why is blood slowest in the smallest vessels?

scenes.tts: Two quantities matter here. Volume flow is how much blood passes a point. Velocity is how fast the blood moves. At steady state, every litre that leaves the aorta passes through the capillaries. So the volume flow through all the capillaries together equals the flow through the aorta.

scenes.visual: Two labelled cards, volume flow and velocity; then the same flow value rides from the aorta to the capillary bed with an equals sign.
scenes.narration: Two quantities matter here. Volume flow is how much blood passes a point. Velocity is how fast the blood moves. At steady state, every litre that leaves the aorta passes through the capillaries. So the volume flow through all the capillaries together equals the flow through the aorta.

scenes.tts: Velocity equals volume flow divided by cross-sectional area. The flow is the same, so a larger area means a lower velocity. Each capillary is tiny. But there are so many side by side that their combined cross-section far exceeds the aorta's. Many tiny tubes in parallel add up to a wide channel.
scenes.visual: The formula appears; a small aorta cross-section square beside a much larger block of many capillary cross-sections, not to scale.

scenes.tts: Here are made-up round numbers for an adult human at rest. Five litres per minute is about 83 cubic centimetres per second. Through an aorta of 4 square centimetres, that is about 21 centimetres per second. Spread over 3,000 square centimetres of capillaries, it is about 0.03 centimetres per second.
scenes.caption: Here are made-up round numbers for an adult human at rest. 5 L/min is about 83 cm³ per second. Through an aorta of 4 cm², that is about 21 cm/s. Spread over 3,000 cm² of capillaries, it is about 0.03 cm/s.
scenes.visual: Two worked lines, 83 divided by 4 and 83 divided by 3,000, with two velocity bars beside them: a tall one and a sliver.

scenes.tts: That slow passage leaves time for exchange. A capillary wall is a single layer of endothelial cells. Little else separates blood from tissue fluid. Blood pressure inside a capillary pushes fluid out. In mammals, plasma proteins pull water back in. The classic textbook model has fluid leaving at the arterial end and returning at the venous end. Reviews conclude that steady return at the venous end lacks reproducible support as a general account. On that view, most tissues filter slowly, and lymph returns the fluid.
scenes.visual: One capillary as a thin-walled bar, blood moving slowly, tissue fluid outside; arrow out labelled pressure, arrow in labelled plasma proteins; then the classic arterial-to-venous picture is dimmed with a note that reviews do not support steady return, and a lymph arrow carries fluid away.

scenes.tts: Keep one rule. Velocity is volume flow divided by cross-sectional area. In adult humans, blood is slowest in the capillaries because together they have the largest cross-section. Each one being narrow is not the reason. Many tiny tubes side by side give a wide channel, and a wide channel means slow blood.
scenes.visual: The aorta and capillary bed side by side again with the formula; the big total area is highlighted, the single narrow tube is crossed out as the explanation.
